title: Orchard accounts
brief: Build a compact retrospective analyst package on a fictional orchard packing cooperative. Each row gives season, crates sold, revenue and operating cost in crowns: 1924 900 7200 6000; 1925 1050 7770 6550; 1926 1200 8160 7120; 1927 980 7644 7130; 1928 1350 9990 8430; 1929 1430 10296 9180. New sorting equipment arrived in late 1927; the accounts do not split varieties or capital expenditure. Explain to the cooperative board what changed in margins and what the records can support. Leave an auditable deliverable. Work only from these fictional figures.

Orchard Packing CooperativeBoard review · 1924–29

The margin recovery peaked in 1928

The cooperative earned an operating surplus in all six seasons. Its margin fell from 16.7% in 1924 to 6.7% in 1927, recovered to 15.6% in 1928, then slipped to 10.8% in 1929 even as crate sales reached their six-season high.

19291,4307.206.421,11610.8%

What moved the margin

From 1924 to 1926, revenue per crate fell from 8.00 to 6.80 crowns. Operating cost per crate fell more slowly, narrowing the surplus on each crate. In 1927 the squeeze came from a different direction. Sales fell by 220 crates while total operating cost edged up by 10 crowns. Cost per crate rose to 7.28 crowns, leaving just 0.52 crowns per crate despite a recovery in revenue per crate.

In 1928 the cooperative sold 370 more crates than in 1927. Revenue per crate fell by 0.40 crowns, but operating cost per crate fell by 1.03. The cooperative earned 1,560 crowns, its largest operating surplus. In 1929 it sold another 80 crates, yet revenue grew by only 306 crowns while costs rose by 750. That reduced the surplus by 444 crowns and the margin by 4.8 percentage points.

What the equipment timing tells us

The new sorter arrived late in 1927. The next two seasons both cleared the 1927 margin, but the annual accounts cannot isolate the sorter’s contribution. They give no within-season comparison, and the missing variety breakdown leaves changes in the mix of crates sold unresolved. Without separate capital expenditure or a measure of savings attributable to the sorter, its payback cannot be calculated.

Download the season ledger (CSV)

The first four columns reproduce the fictional accounts. Operating surplus equals revenue less operating cost. Margin is surplus divided by revenue, expressed as a percentage. Each per-crate figure divides the corresponding season total by crates sold. Figures are rounded after calculation.

Board retrospective · 1924–1929

Orchard Packing Cooperative

Operating margin fell from 16.67% in 1924 to 6.72% in 1927, rebounded to 15.62% in 1928, and slipped to 10.84% in 1929. The rebound followed the late-1927 arrival of new sorting equipment. The accounts establish the timing and the change in recorded costs, while the equipment’s contribution remains unknown.

Operating margin by season

  • 1924
    16.67%
  • 1925
    15.70%
  • 1926
    12.75%
  • 1927
    6.72%
  • 1928
    15.62%
  • 1929
    10.84%

Bars start at zero. Sorting equipment arrived in late 1927.

What changed

1924–26 decline. Revenue per crate fell from 8.00 to 6.80 crowns. Cost per crate also fell, but by less, and the margin narrowed even as crates sold increased.

1927 trough. From 1926, crates fell by 220 and cost per crate rose from 5.93 to 7.28 crowns. Higher revenue per crate only partly offset the cost increase and lower volume.

1928 recovery. Surplus rose by 1,046 crowns. The largest contribution in the surplus bridge came from lower recorded operating cost per crate. Volume rose, while revenue per crate fell.

1929 pullback. Crates reached a six-season high of 1,430. Lower revenue per crate and higher operating cost per crate outweighed the volume gain. Surplus fell by 444 crowns from 1928 and ended 84 crowns below 1924.

What the records support

The pooled 1928–29 margin was 13.19%, or 1.77 percentage points below 1924–26. The post-arrival seasons improved on the 1927 trough, and both remained below the 1924 margin. The pooled comparison places 1927 on its own because the equipment arrived late that year.

Pooled margins use total surplus divided by total revenue within each period.

The six annual totals provide no comparison that isolates the sorter’s effect. The accounts do not break out varieties, so changes in average revenue per crate cannot be separated into selling-price and variety-mix effects. Changes in operating cost per crate also cannot be assigned to sorting efficiency from these totals. Capital spending is not separately identified, so the records cannot establish the equipment’s full cost, payback, or return on investment.

Surplus bridge and audit trail

Change in operating surplus, in crowns. Positive contributions raise surplus.
SeasonsCrate volume Revenue per crateOperating cost per crate Surplus change

  • Operating surplus = revenue − operating cost. Operating margin = 100 × surplus ÷ revenue.
  • Volume contribution = change in crates × starting surplus per crate.
  • Revenue contribution = ending crates × (ending revenue per crate − starting revenue per crate).
  • Cost contribution = ending crates × (starting cost per crate − ending cost per crate).

The bridge values the change in volume at starting rates and applies the change in unit rates to ending volume. Contributions reconcile to the observed surplus change before display rounding. They describe changes in the accounts without attributing them to the sorter.
